d: Mover constraints apply force or torque to move one or more assemblies.
h:
import ConstraintVisualization from '../includes/studio/constraint-visualization.md' import ConstraintSimulation from '../includes/studio/constraint-simulation.md'

The physics engine includes the following Constraints that apply force or torque to move one or more assemblies. In addition, various mechanical constraints are available which behave as conceptual mechanical connections, including hinges, springs, ropes, and more.

Linear Velocity

Angular Velocity

Align Position

Align Orientation

Vector Force

Torque

Line Force

Animation Constraint

Constraint visualization

Create constraints

Mover constraints typically connect one or two Attachments or Bones. When connected to Bones, the constraint will use their animated position and orientation.

To create a mechanical constraint, you can either insert one from the Constraint picker/button or through the Explorer window.

  1. In Studio's Model tab toolbar, click‑hold over the small corner arrow on a constraint button to open its picker menu, then select the desired constraint.

  1. In the 3D viewport, hover over any Part or MeshPart and click to add a new Attachment to the part at the visualized point. Alternatively, hover over and click an existing Attachment or Bone to use it for the constraint.

  2. Some mover constraints utilize or support a secondary attachment in their functionality, so the tool might prompt you to repeat the previous step on another Part, MeshPart, or Attachment, or Bone.

  1. In the Explorer hierarchy, hover over the intended parent, click the ⊕ button, and insert the desired constraint from the dropdown menu, such as a LinearVelocity constraint.

  1. With the new constraint selected, locate its currently empty Attachment0 property in the Properties window.

  1. Link the Attachment0 property to an Attachment or Bone in two consecutive steps:

  2. In the Properties window, click in the Attachment0 row to reveal the selection cursor.

  3. In the Explorer hierarchy, click on the target Attachment or Bone.

  1. Some mover constraints use or support a secondary Attachment or Bone in their functionality. If necessary, repeat the previous step on the Attachment1 property in the Properties window. For instance:

  2. By default, AlignPosition and AlignOrientation align their primary attachment (Attachment0) with a secondary attachment (Attachment1).

  3. LineForce requires two attachments to apply force along the theoretical line connecting them.

Physical simulation

Legacy mover conversion

If your game relies on legacy BodyMover‑based constraints, review the following notes when converting to modern mover constraints.

`BodyPosition`  ⟩  `AlignPosition`

AlignPosition satisfies the majority of use cases covered by the deprecated BodyPosition mover. To sync with how the legacy mover treated each component independently and allowed a different force along each dimension, the ForceLimitMode property of AlignPosition allows the constraint to operate in Magnitude mode or PerAxis mode:

  • In Magnitude mode, the existing behavior is preserved and MaxForce is interpreted as a magnitude.

  • In PerAxis mode, the force along each axis can be specified independently. Because the maximum force is specified as a vector, the reference frame of the force can also be specified through the ForceRelativeTo property with World, Attachment0, and Attachment1 options. Additionally, the formulation for the internal controller is modified to match that of BodyPosition.

`BodyGyro`  ⟩  `AlignOrientation`

AlignOrientation satisfies the majority of use cases covered by the deprecated BodyGyro mover. The AlignType modes of AlignOrientation provide sufficient freedom for most applications and the combination of multiple constraints can replicate the vector torque limit. Additionally, the PrimaryAxisLookAt mode forces the primary axis of the constraint's first attachment (Attachment0) to always point towards the second attachment (Attachment1), making it a lot easier to add things such as motion tracking security cameras or guided missiles.

`BodyVelocity`  ⟩  `LinearVelocity`

LinearVelocity satisfies the majority of use cases covered by the deprecated BodyVelocity mover. Although the legacy mover allows for a MaxForce vector, the typical application of that vector force was to zero a particular component, allowing the constraint to be disabled along that dimension. LinearVelocity achieves a similar effect by operating in distinct VelocityConstraintMode modes that corresponded to one (Line), two (Plane), and three (Vector) dimensions.

Additionally, the ForceLimitMode property with the option of PerAxis accommodates any applications of the vector force with all non‑zero components, such as an increase in the force along a single axis to counteract gravity.

`BodyAngularVelocity`  ⟩  `AngularVelocity`

Although AngularVelocity has some discrepancies with the deprecated BodyAngularVelocity mover, specific cases related to those discrepancies have not been highlighted by the community, nor internally.

As a separate improvement, AngularVelocity works with Attachments and the RelativeTo property lets you specify the CFrame in which the force is specified, for example World or Attachment1.

`BodyForce`/`BodyThrust`  ⟩  `VectorForce`

VectorForce satisfies all use cases offered by the deprecated BodyForce and BodyThrust movers. The modern constraint works with Attachments and its RelativeTo property lets you apply force to a relative offset from center, similar to how BodyThrust.Location worked.

`RocketPropulsion`  ⟩  `LineForce`/`AlignOrientation`

A combination of LineForce and AlignOrientation satisfies the majority of use cases covered by the deprecated RocketPropulsion mover. In the example of a guided missile, LineForce can be used to control the "follow target" behavior of RocketPropulsion while AlignOrientation and its LookAtPosition property can be used to control the "face target" behavior.

kid.simple: Mover constraints are physics tools that push, spin or steer assemblies. They can set a speed (LinearVelocity, AngularVelocity), pull something to a spot or rotation (AlignPosition, AlignOrientation), or apply a steady push or twist (VectorForce, Torque, LineForce). They are how you make hovering platforms, rockets, homing missiles and custom vehicles. This page also explains which modern movers replace the old Body movers like BodyVelocity.
kid.analogy: Mechanical constraints are like the hinges and ropes on a machine. Mover constraints are like the engine, thrusters and steering wheel that actually make it go.
keyPoints: The mover constraints are LinearVelocity, AngularVelocity, AlignPosition, AlignOrientation, VectorForce, Torque, LineForce and AnimationConstraint.
Most use one or two attachments. AlignPosition and AlignOrientation line up Attachment0 with Attachment1 by default, and LineForce needs two attachments.
Create them from the Model tab's constraint picker or by inserting one in the Explorer and setting Attachment0 (and Attachment1 if needed).

Old Body movers are deprecated. BodyPosition becomes AlignPosition, BodyGyro becomes AlignOrientation, BodyVelocity becomes LinearVelocity, BodyAngularVelocity becomes AngularVelocity, and BodyForce or BodyThrust become VectorForce.
RocketPropulsion is replaced by LineForce (to chase a target) plus AlignOrientation (to face it).
AlignOrientation's PrimaryAxisLookAt mode always points Attachment0 at Attachment1, which is great for security cameras or guided missiles.
`RelativeTo` settings choose whether a force is measured in world directions or in an attachment's own directions.

terms.mover constraint: A constraint that adds force or torque to move assemblies.
terms.attachment: A Roblox object you put inside a part to mark one exact point on it. Its Position is measured from the part's center, so an attachment at (0, 3, 0) sits 3 studs above the center of its part.
terms.force: A push or pull in a direction. To hold up a mass of 5.6 against gravity (196.2), you need an upward force of 5.6 x 196.2 = about 1099.
terms.torque: A twisting force that makes things spin.
terms.velocity: Speed with a direction, in studs per second. (0, 0, -10) means 10 studs per second toward negative Z.
terms.align: To pull something into a matching position or rotation.
terms.assembly: Parts joined together that physics moves as one object.
terms.deprecated / legacy: Old features that still exist but should not be used for new work. Roblox recommends the newer replacements.
terms.RelativeTo / ActuatorRelativeTo: Which directions a force uses. World means the world's X, Y, Z (Y is always up). Attachment0 means the attachment's own arrows, so the force turns when the part turns, like a rocket's thrust.
terms.ForceLimitMode: Whether the maximum force is one total limit (Magnitude) or a separate limit for each of X, Y and Z (PerAxis).
terms.VelocityConstraintMode: Whether LinearVelocity controls speed along a line (1 direction), a plane (2 directions) or a full vector (all 3).
terms.center of mass: The balance point of the assembly. A force there pushes it without making it spin.

example.title: A hover block that floats up slowly with VectorForce
example.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local block = Instance.new("Part")
block.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)       -- volume 8, Plastic: mass 5.6
block.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 40)
block.Parent = Workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = block

local thruster = Instance.new("VectorForce")
thruster.Attachment0 = attachment
thruster.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World  -- "up" always means world up
thruster.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true                   -- push without spinning it

-- Weight = mass x gravity = 5.6 x 196.2 = about 1098.7
local weight = block.AssemblyMass * Workspace.Gravity

-- 100% of the weight: it floats in place
thruster.Force = Vector3.new(0, weight, 0)
thruster.Parent = block

task.wait(3)
-- 120% of the weight: the extra 20% makes it rise
thruster.Force = Vector3.new(0, weight * 1.2, 0)
explain: The block is 4 x 1 x 2 = 8 cubic studs of Plastic (density 0.7), so its mass is 5.6.
Gravity is 196.2 studs per second squared, so its weight is 5.6 x 196.2, about 1098.7. We calculate it with `AssemblyMass * Workspace.Gravity` so it still works if you change the size.
An upward force equal to the weight cancels gravity, so the block hovers.
At 120% of the weight, the extra force is about 219.7. Divided by the mass of 5.6, that speeds the block up by about 39.2 studs per second, every second, so it rises faster and faster.
`RelativeTo = World` keeps the force pointing straight up even if the block tips. `ApplyAtCenterOfMass` pushes at the balance point so it does not start spinning.

watchOut: Do not use BodyVelocity, BodyPosition, BodyGyro or BodyForce in new games. Use the modern movers listed above.
A VectorForce never stops pushing. A force bigger than the weight keeps speeding the part up forever. For a steady speed, use LinearVelocity instead.
Forgetting `ApplyAtCenterOfMass` (or putting the attachment off-center) can make the part flip and spin.
If the part moves the wrong way after it rotates, check `RelativeTo`: World directions never turn, attachment directions turn with the part.
